steps.text: DNA contains deoxyribonucleotides linked by 3′–5′ phosphodiester bonds. The two strands of a typical duplex run in opposite directions.
A pairs with T and G with C in canonical DNA base pairing. Hydrogen bonding and base stacking contribute to duplex stability; sequence and conditions both matter.
A strand written 5′-AGTC-3′ pairs with 3′-TCAG-5′. When both are written 5′ to 3′, the complementary sequence is the reverse complement, 5′-GACT-3′.
Denaturation separates paired strands without necessarily hydrolyzing the covalent backbone. GC content influences melting behavior, but salt and length also matter.

steps.text: Eukaryotic DNA wraps around histone proteins to form nucleosomes. Packaging compacts DNA while allowing regulated access for replication, repair and transcription.
Histone tails can receive chemical modifications that influence binding partners and accessibility. The effect depends on the specific modification and genomic context.
Euchromatin is generally more accessible than heterochromatin. This comparison is not a rule that every gene in one region is always on or always off.
Chromatin state is part of gene regulation. A change in transcription can reflect altered access even without changing the underlying DNA sequence.

steps.text: DNA polymerases extend a preexisting strand by adding to its 3′ hydroxyl. New DNA synthesis proceeds 5′ to 3′ while the template is read 3′ to 5′.
At a replication fork, the leading strand is synthesized more continuously toward fork movement. The lagging strand is assembled as Okazaki fragments.
Primase supplies primers; primer removal, gap filling and ligation complete the daughter strand. Ligase seals a nick rather than synthesizing an entire fragment.
Semiconservative replication gives each daughter duplex one parental strand and one newly synthesized strand. Leading and lagging describe local fork geometry.

steps.text: Replication proofreading and postreplicative repair improve fidelity through different steps. A mismatch is not the same lesion as a chemically damaged base.
Base-excision repair removes selected damaged bases before processing the backbone and filling the gap. Nucleotide-excision repair removes a segment containing a bulky lesion.
Mismatch repair corrects some replication errors that escaped proofreading. Accurate repair requires an appropriate template or strand discrimination mechanism.
Double-strand breaks can be processed by homologous recombination or end joining. These mechanisms differ in template use and error risk; repair is not always error-free.

steps.text: PCR amplifies a bounded DNA region using primers, thermal strand separation and a thermostable polymerase. Primers define the region and supply extendable 3′ ends.
Restriction enzymes recognize particular sequences and cleave DNA. Compatible ends can be joined by ligase, but successful insertion does not guarantee correct orientation or expression.
In ideal PCR, copies double each cycle, giving N0 times 2 to the cycle number. Real reactions eventually depart from ideal doubling as reagents and efficiency change.
Sequence confirmation tests the construct directly. A band of the expected size supports an amplicon’s length but does not prove every base is correct.
